:::{#rem-sufficient-meaning}
#### What sufficiency says

Once we know $\statf{\vX}$, the remaining randomness in the sample
has the same distribution whatever the parameter is,
so the sample carries no further information about $\param$ beyond $\statf{\vX}$.
A statistic can therefore stand in for the whole sample when we estimate $\param$.

The sample itself, taking $\statf{\vX} = \vX$, is always sufficient but does not reduce the data;
a useful sufficient statistic is a much shorter summary,
such as a sum or a mean.

Sufficiency by itself does not give a best estimator:
it says which summaries lose nothing, not which function of them to use.
The Rao--Blackwell theorem below shows how to improve a given unbiased estimator.

For a continuous sample, the definition, the factorization theorem and the conditional expectations below
use densities and integrals instead of probability mass functions and sums.
:::
